explanation: A binary operation must return one element of the same set for every ordered pair. Associativity changes brackets, not order. Integer addition, nonzero real multiplication, and invertible matrix multiplication are examples. Matrices of determinant 1 form the special linear group.
intuition: Composition is the basic operation: make one move, then another. The group axioms guarantee that moves combine consistently and can be undone.
pitfall: A Latin square is necessary for a finite group table, but does not by itself establish associativity. Zero has no multiplicative inverse.
prompt: Compose a rotation with a reflection in both orders. Which axiom allows regrouping three moves?
proof: Matrix multiplication is associative. The identity matrix is in both sets. Determinants multiply, giving closure, and det(A⁻¹)=det(A)⁻¹ gives closure under inverses.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_01.pdf

title: A group is a calculus of reversible moves

definition: o(g)=\min\{m\ge1:g^m=e\},\qquad o(g)=\infty\ \text{if this set is empty}
explanation: The identity and each inverse are unique. Cancellation is allowed on a fixed side. Inverting a product reverses its order. Conjugation changes the frame in which a move is described and preserves its order. Group order counts elements; element order counts repetitions.
intuition: An inverse reverses a move; the order counts how many repeated applications first return to the identity.
pitfall: Two infinite groups need not have the same cardinality. Also (ab)^m=a^mb^m requires a commutativity hypothesis.
prompt: Select an element and follow its successive powers until the identity first appears.
proof: If u and v are inverses of g, then u=u(gv)=(ug)v=v. Multiply an equality on the appropriate side to cancel. Since (hgh⁻¹)^m=hg^mh⁻¹, precisely the same positive exponents yield the identity.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_01.pdf

title: Identity, inverses, cancellation and order

definition: H\le G\iff H\ne\varnothing\ \text{and}\ xy^{-1}\in H\quad(\forall x,y\in H)
explanation: The operation is inherited from the ambient group. Every subgroup contains the ambient identity. Intersections of subgroups are subgroups; unions generally are not. Every subgroup of the additive integers consists of all multiples of one nonnegative integer.
intuition: A subgroup is a collection of moves that remains self-contained when moves are composed or reversed.
pitfall: A subset of the correct size need not be a subgroup. Closure under products alone suffices for a nonempty finite subset, but not an infinite one.
prompt: Choose proposed generators and inspect which subset closes under multiplication.
proof: For the subgroup test, choose x=y to obtain e, then e·y⁻¹ for inverses and x·(y⁻¹)⁻¹ for products. For integers, choose the least positive member m of a nonzero subgroup and divide every other member by m; minimality forces zero remainder.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_01.pdf

theorem: H\le(\mathbb Z,+)\Longrightarrow H=m\mathbb Z\ (m\ge0),\qquad b\mathbb Z\le a\mathbb Z\iff a\mid b
title: Closed worlds inside a group

definition: \langle S\rangle=\bigcap_{\substack{H\le G\\S\subseteq H}}H=\{s_1^{\varepsilon_1}\cdots s_k^{\varepsilon_k}:s_i\in S,\ \varepsilon_i=\pm1,\ k\ge0\}
explanation: The empty word is the identity. Adding generators can only enlarge the generated subgroup. A subgroup lattice records inclusion, not geometric position: meet is intersection and join is the subgroup generated by both sets. Integer generation is governed by the greatest common divisor.
intuition: Generators are a small vocabulary of moves. Their finite words describe every move that those generators can reach.
pitfall: Joining two subgroups means generating from their union; the union itself can fail closure.
prompt: Compare the subgroups generated by a rotation, a reflection, and both together.
proof: Every integer combination of a and b is divisible by their gcd. Bézout's identity expresses the gcd itself as an integer combination, so the generated subgroup contains all its multiples and nothing else.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_01.pdf

title: Generators and the subgroup lattice

definition: a\equiv b\pmod n\iff a-b\in n\mathbb Z,\qquad [a]+[b]=[a+b]
explanation: For n≥1 there are n residue classes. Representatives are labels for whole classes, not new elements. Addition and multiplication are well-defined because replacing representatives by multiples of n changes their sum and product only by multiples of n. The additive group is cyclic.
intuition: Residues forget whole turns around a clock while retaining enough information to add consistently.
pitfall: Equality of classes is not equality of their representatives. Modulo 0 means equality, giving a copy of the integers rather than a finite clock.
prompt: Change the clock size and watch different integer representatives land at the same residue.
proof: If a'=a+kn and b'=b+ℓn, then a'+b' differs from a+b by (k+ℓ)n. The class of 0 is the identity, and the class of −a is the inverse of the class of a.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_02.pdf

title: Congruence folds the integer line into a clock

explanation: Use n≥2 here. A unit is a residue with a multiplicative inverse. Bézout's identity turns a gcd calculation into an inverse calculation. For prime p every nonzero residue is a unit. Composite moduli may have nonzero nonunits, so multiplication on all residues is not a group.
intuition: Some residues undo multiplication and some do not. The invertible residues form their own group.
pitfall: Additive order and multiplicative order are different quantities. The unit group of a composite modulus need not be cyclic.
prompt: For modulus 8, compare the order of each unit with the orders in a cyclic group of size 4.
proof: Bézout gives au+nv=1 exactly when gcd(a,n)=1; reducing modulo n exhibits u as an inverse. Conversely any congruence au≡1 mod n forces every common divisor of a and n to divide 1.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_02.pdf

title: Units and the totient function

definition: D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=e,\ srs=r^{-1}\rangle=\{r^is^j:0\le i<n,\ j\in\{0,1\}\}
explanation: The course convention is that D_n has 2n elements. Here r rotates counterclockwise through 2π/n and s reflects in the horizontal axis, with one vertex initially at (1,0). Composition applies the rightmost operation first. There are n rotations and n reflections.
intuition: Every polygon symmetry is determined by where one vertex goes and which way the next vertex lies.
pitfall: Some books call this same group D₂ₙ. A reflection cannot be continuously connected to a rotation through orthogonal matrices of the plane.
prompt: Build a word, reverse its order, and compare the labeled vertices and matrix products.
proof: The relation sr=r⁻¹s moves every reflection to the right, reducing any word to the displayed form. A symmetry has n choices for the image of a chosen vertex and two for the adjacent vertex; these 2n forms realize all possibilities.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_02.pdf

title: The symmetries of a regular polygon

explanation: Follow a label until it returns to find a cycle, then repeat on unused labels. The resulting disjoint cycles are unique up to cyclic relabeling and reordering. Disjoint cycles commute; overlapping cycles usually do not. Inverse cycles run backward.
intuition: A permutation routes labels. Disjoint cycles are independent loops in that routing.
pitfall: The lcm formula applies to a decomposition into disjoint cycles. It need not hold for an arbitrary product of overlapping cycles.
prompt: Trace a label through two permutations in both orders and read the final disjoint cycles.
proof: A power of a disjoint-cycle permutation fixes every point exactly when that power is divisible by every cycle length. The smallest such positive exponent is their least common multiple.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_02.pdf

title: Permutations, cycles and composition

definition: \langle g\rangle=\{g^k:k\in\mathbb Z\},\qquad C_n\cong\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z,\qquad C_\infty\cong\mathbb Z
explanation: All cyclic groups are abelian. A finite group is cyclic exactly when it contains an element whose order is the whole group order. Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic; for each divisor d of n there is one subgroup of C_n of order d.
intuition: Repeating one move produces either a closed loop or an unending chain. These are the only cyclic possibilities.
pitfall: An abelian group need not be cyclic. A cycle in an arbitrary drawing need not mean the group itself is cyclic.
prompt: On C₁₂, choose step sizes 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6. Explain every orbit length using the gcd.
proof: The equality (g^k)^m=e means n divides km. Dividing n and k by their gcd shows that the least positive m is n/gcd(n,k). The map k↦g^k has kernel nℤ in the finite case and zero kernel in the infinite case.

source.title: MH2220_Course_Notes_2025.pdf
source.section: 2.4 Cyclic group I; 3.2 Cyclic group II

title: Cyclic groups and the arithmetic of powers

explanation: A homomorphism sends identity to identity and inverses to inverses. Its image is a subgroup; its kernel records moves invisible in the target. Composition of homomorphisms remains a homomorphism. Determinant maps GL_n(F) to the multiplicative group F×, with kernel SL_n(F).
intuition: A homomorphism translates one language of moves into another without changing how compositions behave.
pitfall: A determinant map has codomain F× under multiplication, not all of F as a multiplicative group. An arbitrary labeling need not preserve products.
prompt: Choose a map and compare translating a product with multiplying the two translated elements.
proof: From φ(e)=φ(e)², cancel to obtain φ(e)=e. Apply φ to gg⁻¹=e for inverses. For k in the kernel, φ(gkg⁻¹)=φ(g)eφ(g)⁻¹=e, establishing normality.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

title: Homomorphisms preserve composition

explanation: The labels and geometric realization may change while the algebra remains identical. Isomorphisms preserve element orders, group order, commutativity, cyclicity and subgroup structure. Comparing these invariants can disprove a proposed isomorphism, though matching a few invariants does not establish one.
intuition: Two groups are isomorphic when a bijective relabeling matches every multiplication entry.
pitfall: Groups of equal size need not be isomorphic. Identical-looking Cayley graphs without edge labels do not prove an isomorphism.
prompt: Match the polygon rotations to residues and check that each table entry is preserved.
proof: A bijective homomorphism satisfies φ(g)^m=e exactly when g^m=e, so element orders agree. C₄ has an element of order 4, whereas every nonidentity element of C₂×C₂ has order 2.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

theorem: G\cong H\Longrightarrow o(g)=o(\phi(g)),\qquad C_4\not\cong C_2\times C_2
title: Isomorphism means the same multiplication

explanation: The jth column is the image of the jth basis vector. Permutation matrices have one 1 in each row and column. This construction is faithful: different permutations give different matrices. It is the first bridge from a group action to a linear representation.
intuition: Replace each label by a basis vector. Routing labels now becomes a linear transformation.
pitfall: Switching between row-vector and column-vector conventions reverses composition conventions unless handled consistently.
prompt: Select a permutation and watch each basis vector move to the column shown in its matrix.
proof: Apply both sides of the product identity to each basis vector: PσPτe_j=e_{σ(τ(j))}. The columns are an orthonormal basis, so the transpose is the inverse, and taking determinants gives determinant squared equal to 1.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

title: A permutation becomes a matrix

explanation: A k-cycle can be expressed as k−1 transpositions, giving sign (−1)^(k−1). The sign of a product is the product of signs, even for overlapping cycles. Thus every transposition decomposition has the same parity. A_n contains the even permutations.
intuition: Parity extracts one bit from a permutation: whether its matrix preserves or reverses orientation.
pitfall: The sign is not (−1) raised to the total number of cycles; a cycle contributes −1 exactly when its length is even. A₁ has order 1.
prompt: Change a cycle length and compare its determinant with the predicted parity.
proof: Multiplicativity follows from determinant. Multiplying by a fixed transposition gives a bijection between even and odd permutations, so precisely half are even when n≥2.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

title: Parity and the alternating group

definition: gH=\{gh:h\in H\},\qquad Hg=\{hg:h\in H\},\qquad gH=kH\iff k^{-1}g\in H
explanation: Left cosets partition the group, and each has the same size as H. Right cosets form another partition. In a nonabelian group the two partitions need not agree. A coset usually is not itself a subgroup because it may not contain the identity.
intuition: A coset is a translated copy of a subgroup. Distinct copies fit together without overlap.
pitfall: Elements of G/H are whole cosets. At this stage G/H is a set; it is a quotient group only when H is normal.
prompt: Compare left and right cosets of a reflection subgroup in D₃.
proof: If gh=kh', then k⁻¹g=h'h⁻¹ lies in H, which implies gH=kH. Left multiplication by g is a bijection from H to gH, with inverse multiplication by g⁻¹.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

title: Cosets tile a group

explanation: The index counts cosets. In a finite group, subgroup order and every element order divide group order. A group of prime order is necessarily cyclic. Lagrange restricts possible subgroup sizes but does not promise a subgroup for each divisor.
intuition: Counting a finite group by equal-size coset tiles turns subgroup structure into divisibility.
pitfall: The converse fails: A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6. A subset whose size divides |G| need not be closed.
prompt: Select a subgroup and verify that the number of cosets times their size equals the group order.
proof: Cosets partition G and each has |H| elements, giving the formula. Apply it to the cyclic subgroup generated by g. If |G| is prime, any nonidentity element has order p and generates the whole group.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

title: Lagrange counts identical tiles

explanation: Euler's theorem applies to units modulo n. Fermat's little theorem is its prime-modulus specialization. The coprimality condition matters: for a nonunit, repeated multiplication need not return to 1.
intuition: Two famous congruences become instances of a single fact: an element order divides its finite group order.
pitfall: The congruence a^(p−1)≡1 is not valid for a divisible by p. The version a^p≡a mod p includes that case.
prompt: Choose a unit and track its powers. Compare its actual order with the totient bound.
proof: Apply Lagrange to the element [a] of the finite unit group. For prime p there are exactly p−1 nonzero residues and every one is a unit.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

theorem: a^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod n;\qquad a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\quad(p\text{ prime},\ p\nmid a)
title: Euler and Fermat from a finite group

explanation: The cyclic groups provide one example at each order. At order 4, absence of an element of order 4 forces every nonidentity element to square to the identity, giving the Klein four-group. At order 6, the nonabelian possibility is the symmetry group of a triangle.
intuition: Small orders leave little room for different multiplication structures, but equal cardinality already stops being decisive at order 4.
pitfall: Classification lists isomorphism types, not every possible naming of their elements. Similar diagrams do not collapse different types.
prompt: Compare C₄ and the Klein four-group by their element-order distributions.
proof: Proof idea: Lagrange restricts possible element orders. For order 6, one finds elements a,b of orders 2,3. If they commute they generate C₆; otherwise conjugation by a inverts b, yielding the dihedral relations.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

theorem: S_3\cong D_3\cong C_3\rtimes C_2,\qquad C_6\not\cong S_3
title: Classifying the first few group orders

explanation: Each row of a Cayley table lists a permutation of the group. Left multiplication is faithful because its effect on the identity already recovers the acting element. Hence every finite group of order n occurs inside S_n.
intuition: Let each group element act by left multiplication on the entire group. The multiplication table turns into a collection of permutations.
pitfall: The embedding need not use the smallest possible symmetric group. Do not confuse the regular action on |G| elements with a polygon's action on its vertices.
prompt: Read each multiplication-table row as a permutation and compare products of those permutations.
proof: Left multiplication by g⁻¹ is the inverse of λ_g. Associativity gives λ_gλ_h(x)=g(hx)=(gh)x. If λ_g is the identity permutation, then g=λ_g(e)=e.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_03.pdf

title: Every finite group permutes itself

definition: N\trianglelefteq G\iff gNg^{-1}=N\ \forall g\in G\iff gN=Ng\ \forall g\in G
explanation: Normality is invariance of a whole set under conjugation. It does not say that each element stays fixed. Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal. Every subgroup of index 2 is normal because the only other left or right coset is its complement.
intuition: A normal subgroup is unchanged when its moves are described after a change of frame.
pitfall: Setwise equality gN=Ng does not imply gn=ng for every n. Normal subgroups need not lie in the center.
prompt: Conjugate a reflection subgroup, then the rotation subgroup, and observe which set remains unchanged.
proof: For index 2, if g lies in N both cosets equal N. If g does not, both gN and Ng equal G\N. Thus left and right cosets agree for every g.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

title: Normality means invariance under conjugation

explanation: Replacing a move by another in its coset should not change the resulting coset of a product. Normality is exactly the condition that makes the induced multiplication independent of representatives. Quotients of abelian groups are abelian, and quotients of cyclic groups are cyclic.
intuition: A quotient remembers only which coset a move belongs to. Multiplication survives when that forgetting is consistent.
pitfall: Removing the elements of N from G does not form G/N. The identity in the quotient is the entire coset N.
prompt: Collapse the rotations of D₄ to one coset and identify the two-element quotient.
proof: If g'=gn and h'=hm with n,m in N, then g'h'=gh(h⁻¹nh)m, which lies in ghN because h⁻¹nh lies in N. Associativity, identity and inverses descend from G.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

title: Quotient groups identify invisible moves

definition: \mathbb R/\mathbb Z\cong S^1=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\},\qquad t+\mathbb Z\longmapsto e^{2\pi i t}
explanation: Addition of real parameters becomes multiplication on the unit circle. Choosing t in [0,1) is a way to pick one representative per coset; the interval itself is not closed under ordinary addition. This is also the rotation group SO(2), through the usual rotation matrix.
intuition: Wrap the real line around a circle. Points separated by an integer land at exactly the same place.
pitfall: This is an infinite continuous group. A finite polygon samples only finitely many rotations and is not all of SO(2).
prompt: Advance the angle through several full turns and observe the same circle position with different real representatives.
proof: The exponential identity gives the homomorphism. Equality of unit complex numbers is equivalent to arguments differing by an integer multiple of 2π, proving that the fibers are exactly cosets of ℤ and that the displayed map is bijective.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

theorem: e^{2\pi i(s+t)}=e^{2\pi is}e^{2\pi it},\qquad e^{2\pi is}=e^{2\pi it}\iff s-t\in\mathbb Z
title: The real line modulo one turn

explanation: Automorphisms form a group under composition. Conjugations form its normal subgroup of inner automorphisms. An automorphism that is not inner is called outer. For a cyclic group, sending g to g^k is an automorphism precisely when k is coprime to the group order.
intuition: An automorphism reorganizes a group internally while preserving all multiplication. For a cyclic group, it is a choice of a new generator.
pitfall: The set of outer automorphisms is generally not a subgroup. The outer automorphism group is the quotient Aut(G)/Inn(G).
prompt: On C₈, test the exponent maps k=1,3,5,7 and compose them.
proof: An automorphism is determined by the image of a generator, and that image must again generate. Composing g↦g^k and g↦g^ℓ multiplies k and ℓ modulo n. The homomorphism g↦c_g has kernel exactly the center, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the second identity.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

title: Automorphisms and changes of generators

explanation: The center consists of moves commuting with everything. The centralizer of a subgroup fixes it pointwise by conjugation, while the normalizer fixes it setwise. The normalizer is the largest subgroup of G in which H is normal.
intuition: Centralizing fixes every relevant move individually; normalizing preserves a whole subgroup while possibly rearranging its elements.
pitfall: Normalizer and centralizer need not be equal. If G/Z(G) is cyclic, G is abelian: write each element as a power of one lift times a central element.
prompt: Choose generators for H and a conjugating element b. Compare bHb⁻¹, the centralizer size and the normalizer size. When is H normal?
proof: Conjugation gives a homomorphism from N_G(H) to Aut(H). Its kernel consists exactly of elements commuting with every member of H, namely C_G(H). The first isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient with its image.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

title: Centers, centralizers and normalizers

explanation: For finite-order elements the order formula follows by returning both coordinates to identity. Internally, G is the direct product of H and K if G=HK, H∩K={e}, and both are normal. Distinct prime-power factors of a cyclic group separate into independent coordinates.
intuition: In a direct product, two coordinates move independently. Their repetitions synchronize according to a least common multiple.
pitfall: The Cartesian set alone does not determine a direct product. C₂×C₂ is not cyclic even though it has four elements.
prompt: Compare the orbit of (1,1) in C₂×C₃ with its orbit in C₂×C₄.
proof: The element (1,1) in additive C_m×C_n has order lcm(m,n), which equals mn exactly in the coprime case. When both subgroups are normal with trivial intersection, their commutators lie in the intersection, so the coordinates commute and multiplication H×K→G is an isomorphism.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

title: Independent coordinates and the Chinese remainder pattern

explanation: The action homomorphism α is part of the data. A trivial action gives the direct product. In D_n, the reflection coordinate acts on the rotation coordinate by inversion, explaining the sign change in its multiplication formula. Internally one requires a normal subgroup N and a complement H.
intuition: A semidirect product still has two coordinates, but the second changes how the first is composed.
pitfall: The complement H need not be normal. The same underlying set N×H can support nonisomorphic semidirect products for different actions.
prompt: Compare a direct product with the inversion action. Watch how crossing the reflection coordinate reverses a rotation step.
proof: Every g has a unique expression nh. Multiplying nh and n'h' gives n(hn'h⁻¹)hh', exactly the displayed law. Associativity follows from α(hh')=α(h)α(h').

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_04.pdf

theorem: G=NH,\quad N\trianglelefteq G,\quad N\cap H=\{e\}\Longrightarrow G\cong N\rtimes H;\qquad D_n\cong C_n\rtimes C_2
title: Semidirect products: one coordinate acts on the other

explanation: The subgroup generated by all commutators is normal. Quotienting by it makes every pair commute. This abelianization is the universal part of G visible to homomorphisms into abelian groups.
intuition: The word xyx⁻¹y⁻¹ measures the mismatch between doing x then y and doing them in the opposite order.
pitfall: A commutator subgroup contains products of commutators, not merely the displayed individual commutators. Different books may use the inverse commutator convention.
prompt: Compute the commutator of a rotation and reflection in D₄, then see what survives in the abelian quotient.
proof: Conjugating a commutator gives [gxg⁻¹,gyg⁻¹], so the generated subgroup is normal. The cosets xN and yN commute exactly when [x,y] lies in N. Any homomorphism to an abelian group kills every commutator and therefore factors through G/G'.

source.title: MH2220_Course_Notes_2025.pdf

theorem: G/N\text{ abelian}\iff G'\le N\quad(N\trianglelefteq G),\qquad G^{\mathrm{ab}}=G/G'
title: Commutators measure the failure to commute

explanation: Two elements have the same image exactly when their quotient lies in the kernel. More generally, a map factors uniquely through G/N whenever the normal subgroup N is contained in its kernel. The factor map is injective exactly when nothing more than N is collapsed.
intuition: A homomorphism collapses each kernel coset to a single point. After precisely that collapse, it becomes an isomorphism onto its image.
pitfall: The target is the image, not automatically all of the codomain. A non-surjective map does not yield G/ker φ≅H.
prompt: Map C₆ to C₃ and inspect the two-element fibers before collapsing them.
proof: Equality of kernel cosets is equivalent to φ(g)=φ(h), proving both well-definedness and injectivity of the factor map. Its multiplication law follows from φ, and surjectivity follows from restricting the target to im φ.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_05.pdf

title: The first isomorphism theorem: fibers become points

definition: H,K\le G,\quad K\le N_G(H)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad HK/H\cong K/(H\cap K)
explanation: The normalizer hypothesis makes HK a subgroup and H normal in HK. It also makes H∩K normal in K. In particular the theorem applies whenever H is normal in the whole group G.
intuition: To see what K contributes beyond H, discard the overlap H∩K. The result is the same as adjoining K to H and then quotienting by H.
pitfall: HK is not always a subgroup. Writing HK/H as a quotient group requires the relevant normality conditions.
prompt: Follow the diamond of inclusions. Assume N is normal in G: the map H → HN/N has kernel H∩N. Which two quotient groups must agree?
proof: The displayed map is a homomorphism. Every coset (hk)H equals kH because K normalizes H, so it is onto. Its kernel is K∩H. Apply the first isomorphism theorem. The size formula follows, and in fact holds for any finite subgroups even when HK is only a set.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_05.pdf

theorem: K\to HK/H,\ k\mapsto kH,\qquad \ker=H\cap K,\qquad |HK|=\frac{|H||K|}{|H\cap K|}\quad(G\text{ finite})
title: The second isomorphism theorem: the diamond

definition: N\le H\le G,\quad N,H\trianglelefteq G,\qquad (G/N)/(H/N)\cong G/H
explanation: Both N and H must be normal in G. The map from G/N to G/H sends a smaller coset to the larger coset containing it. Its kernel consists of precisely the smaller cosets lying inside H.
intuition: Forgetting N and then forgetting the rest of H has the same effect as forgetting H at once.
pitfall: Normality of N in H and H in G alone does not imply normality of N in G. Check both required quotient groups exist.
prompt: Follow both routes from G to G/M: quotient directly by M, or first by N and then by M/N. Why does every element reach the same final coset?
proof: If gN=g'N, then g⁻¹g' lies in N⊆H, so gH=g'H. Thus ψ is well-defined; it is a surjective homomorphism. Its kernel is H/N, and the first isomorphism theorem supplies the result.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_05.pdf

title: The third isomorphism theorem: quotient in stages

definition: N\trianglelefteq G,\quad \{H\le G:N\le H\}\longleftrightarrow\{K\le G/N\},\qquad H\mapsto H/N,\quad K\mapsto\pi^{-1}(K)
explanation: Assume N is a normal subgroup of G. The correspondence preserves inclusion and normality. Subgroups that do not contain N have no place in this bijection. For the integers modulo n, divisors of n encode the resulting cyclic subgroup lattice.
intuition: The subgroup lattice of a quotient is the part of the original lattice above the subgroup being collapsed.
pitfall: The theorem does not identify every subgroup of G with a subgroup of G/N. Only those containing N participate.
prompt: Select a normal subgroup, hide lattice nodes below or incomparable with it, and relabel the remaining nodes by their quotients.
proof: The preimage of a subgroup under π is a subgroup containing ker π=N. Conversely π⁻¹(π(H))=H whenever H contains N. These inverse maps preserve inclusion. Conjugation passes through π, giving the equivalence of normality.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_05.pdf

theorem: H\trianglelefteq G\iff H/N\trianglelefteq G/N,\qquad [H:K]=[H/N:K/N]\quad(N\le K\le H)
title: The correspondence theorem: a lattice above the kernel

definition: G\cong\prod_i C_{p_i^{a_i}}\cong C_{d_1}\times\cdots\times C_{d_r},\qquad d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_r
explanation: Here G is finite abelian; the primes in the first product may repeat. These are elementary-divisor and invariant-factor descriptions. With nontrivial factors and standard ordering, the lists are unique. The course writes the invariant factors in the opposite order, an equivalent convention.
intuition: An abelian group splits into independent prime-power clocks. Several clocks for the same prime need not combine into one.
pitfall: The theorem needs both finiteness and commutativity. Having the right total order does not determine the partition of each prime exponent.
prompt: List the three abelian groups of order 8 and compare their maximum element orders.
proof: Proof idea: split G into its p-primary subgroups using Bézout. In an abelian p-group, a cyclic subgroup of maximal order has a complement; induct on the remaining order. Uniqueness can be recovered from the sizes of the subgroups killed by each power of p.

source.title: MH2220_Lecture_Chapter_05.pdf

title: Finite abelian groups decompose into cyclic pieces

definition: Q_8=\langle a,b\mid a^4=e,\ a^2=b^2,\ ba=a^{-1}b\rangle=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}
explanation: In Q₈, i²=j²=k²=ijk=−1. There is exactly one element of order 2, namely −1; the six elements ±i,±j,±k have order 4. Its three cyclic subgroups of order 4 meet in {±1}. Every subgroup of Q₈ is normal.

explanation: Set v(0)=infinity. If t has value 1, every nonzero field element is a unit times an integer power of t. The resulting valuation ring is a local PID and has Krull dimension one. For the rational numbers, counting powers of p gives the localization of the integers at p.
intuition: A discrete valuation measures the exponent of one distinguished prime direction. Units have exponent zero; ideals correspond to lower bounds on that exponent.
pitfall: This additive discrete valuation is different from the Euclidean function called a valuation earlier. The valuation of 0 is a convention outside the map on F×.
prompt: Increase the power of the uniformizer. Watch ideal inclusion reverse the exponent order; compare this infinite descending chain with a finite quotient.
proof: Divide x by t to the power v(x); the quotient and its inverse both have value zero and lie in R, so it is a unit. For a nonzero ideal choose its smallest occurring valuation n; every member is divisible by t^n and an element of valuation n generates the ideal.

title: Discrete valuations: one exponent controls the ideals

explanation: The defining quadratic has no root in the two-element field and is therefore irreducible. Its ideal is maximal, so the quotient is a field. Addition uses binary coefficients; multiplication first expands and then replaces each square of alpha by alpha+1.
intuition: A new algebraic direction can enlarge a finite field without changing its characteristic. Polynomial reduction turns infinitely many expressions into finitely many distinct classes.
pitfall: The four-element field is not integers modulo 4. Its nonzero multiplicative group is cyclic of order 3, whereas its additive group has exponent 2.
prompt: Multiply alpha by alpha+1 and reduce. Then compare the field's two operation tables with those modulo 4.
proof: The quadratic evaluates to 1 at both possible inputs, proving irreducibility. Monic division gives four distinct linear representatives. The displayed inverse relation shows directly that both nonconstant nonzero elements are units, while 1 is its own inverse.
