title: Build a field with four elements
GL and SL: what must a transformation preserve?

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: A matrix is a rule for moving an entire coordinate frame. Invertibility means the frame never collapses; determinant one means its oriented volume is unchanged.
explanation: Here n is a positive integer and F is a field. Over the real numbers, the absolute determinant gives volume scaling and its sign gives orientation. The determinant homomorphism forgets the details of the deformation and remembers one scalar. Special orthogonal matrices preserve both inner products and orientation, a stronger condition than determinant one: a shear can belong to SL without preserving lengths.
proof: The determinant is multiplicative and is onto because diag(a,1,…,1) has determinant a for every nonzero a. Apply the first isomorphism theorem. Over a field of q elements, choose the columns successively: the next column must avoid the span of the previously chosen columns, which contains q^j vectors after j independent choices.
pitfall: Determinant one does not imply orthogonal. Volume language applies to real matrices; the finite-field count uses linear independence rather than Euclidean volume.
prompt: Trace the determinant map and its kernel in the diagram. Compare the conditions defining GL, SL and O in the matrix lab.

title: Flags: a line inside a plane

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §5 Parabolic Subgroups: complete flags and flag stabilizers

intuition: A flag remembers a sequence of nested directions. In three dimensions, preserve a line and then the plane containing it; this forces a triangular pattern in the matrix.
explanation: We use column vectors and left actions throughout. Preserving the first line forces the first column to have only its first entry nonzero. Preserving the first plane forces the third entry of the second column to vanish. Invertibility then makes every diagonal entry nonzero. A partial flag omits some intermediate dimensions; its stabilizer is a parabolic subgroup.
theorem: B=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\0&d&e\\0&0&f\end{pmatrix}:adf\ne0\right\},\qquad \mathrm{GL}_3(F)/B\cong\{\text{complete flags in }F^3\}\quad\text{as sets with an action}.
proof: The column conditions are exactly preservation of each subspace in the standard flag. Every complete flag admits an adapted basis; the matrix with this basis as columns sends the standard flag to it, so the action is transitive. The map gB ↦ g·F₀ is a well-defined equivariant bijection by the stabilizer criterion.
pitfall: This coset space is a set with a GL action, not generally a quotient group: B need not be normal. For row/right conventions the triangular pattern must be translated consistently.
prompt: Follow the nested subspaces and ask which entries of a column-action matrix must vanish at each stage.

title: Maschke: average away a bad choice

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: An arbitrary projection can favor one direction and fail to respect symmetry. Averaging all its symmetry transforms removes that bias and produces a projection that commutes with the group.
explanation: Assume G is finite, V is finite-dimensional over a field F, the characteristic of F does not divide |G|, and W is an invariant subspace. Choose any linear projection onto W. The averaged projection still lands in W and is the identity there, but now its kernel is also invariant. This explains why ordinary complex representations split into irreducible pieces.
proof: Each summand lands in W and fixes every vector of W, so the average does too. Conjugating the average by any ρ(h) merely permutes the summands; thus it commutes with the action. Its kernel is invariant, and every v splits uniquely as P̄v+(v−P̄v), with the second term in the kernel.
pitfall: Finiteness and the invertibility of |G| in F are essential hypotheses for this averaging proof. An invariant subspace alone does not provide an invariant complement for arbitrary groups and fields.
prompt: Use the permutation example: the constant line and the sum-zero plane are both invariant. Relate their direct sum to the averaging argument.

title: Schur: maps between irreducible worlds

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: An equivariant map cannot carve a nontrivial invariant piece out of an irreducible representation. It either loses everything or identifies the whole representation with another.
explanation: Let V and W be nonzero irreducible modules. The kernel and image of an equivariant map are invariant subspaces. Irreducibility therefore leaves only two possibilities for each. Over the complex numbers, finite dimension gives the stronger scalar-endomorphism statement, since an endomorphism has an eigenvalue.
theorem: T\ne0\Longrightarrow T:V\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}W,\qquad \operatorname{End}_G(V)=\mathbb C I_V\quad(V\text{ irreducible, finite-dimensional over }\mathbb C).
proof: If T is nonzero then its kernel cannot be all of V and its image cannot be zero; irreducibility gives ker T=0 and im T=W. For a complex equivariant endomorphism choose an eigenvalue λ. The map T−λI is equivariant and has a nonzero kernel; the first statement forces T−λI=0.
pitfall: The scalar conclusion need not hold over the real numbers. Nonzero vector spaces are required in the definition of irreducibility.
prompt: Compare a nonzero map between irreducible modules with a projection from a reducible module. Which invariant kernel is permitted?

title: Characters: the trace remembers the action

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: A character compresses a matrix into the sum of its eigenvalues. It ignores the chosen coordinates while retaining enough information to distinguish finite-dimensional complex representations of a finite group.
explanation: Throughout this lesson G is finite and representations are finite-dimensional over the complex numbers. Conjugate group elements act by similar matrices, so the character is constant on conjugacy classes. For a permutation representation the trace is exactly the number of basis elements fixed. A geometric three-dimensional trace and a permutation trace on eight vertices are characters of different representations.
proof: Conjugation produces ρ(h)ρ(g)ρ(h)⁻¹, which has the same trace. If g has finite order m then ρ(g) is diagonalizable with mth roots of unity as eigenvalues. The trace bound follows from the triangle inequality. Equality to the positive real number dim V forces every eigenvalue to be 1, so the matrix is the identity.
pitfall: A character value is not generally the number of fixed vectors or the dimension of the fixed subspace. Fixed-point counting applies directly to a permutation basis.
prompt: In the S₃ table, compare the standard character with the three-point permutation character, which is trivial plus standard.

title: Orthogonality turns traces into multiplicities

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory
source.section: §15 The Character Table: row orthogonality; S₃ example

intuition: Irreducible characters act like perpendicular measuring directions. Weight each conjugacy class by its size, take an inner product, and the result tells you how many copies of an irreducible representation are present.
explanation: Let G be finite and all representations finite-dimensional over the complex numbers; χᵢ are its irreducible characters. For S₃ the conjugacy classes have sizes 1, 3 and 2, represented by the identity, a transposition and a three-cycle. In this order the irreducible characters are (1,1,1), (1,−1,1) and (2,0,−1). Their dimensions satisfy 1²+1²+2²=6. The square of the standard character is (4,0,1), so the tensor square contains one copy of each irreducible.
proof: Proof idea for orthogonality: average the group action on Hom(V,W) to project onto equivariant maps. Its trace is the character inner product. Schur’s lemma makes this dimension 1 for equal irreducibles and 0 for distinct ones. Additivity gives the multiplicity formula. For the displayed tensor square, all three weighted inner products are 1, and the dimensions sum to 4.
pitfall: Do not take an unweighted dot product of table rows. Complex conjugation is part of the inner product, even when every entry in this particular table is real.
prompt: Select two S₃ irreducibles to tensor. Check every multiplicity with weights 1, 3, 2 and verify the total dimension.

title: Induction: one copy over every coset

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: A representation of a subgroup describes local symmetry. Induction places a copy of that vector space over each left coset and lets the whole group move the copies, applying a subgroup action whenever the coset representative changes.
explanation: Assume G is finite, H is a subgroup, F is a field and W is a finite-dimensional left FH-module. Choose one representative t for every left coset tH. The tensor relation th⊗w=t⊗hw makes the change of representative consistent. The individual coset copies usually are not G-invariant: the action permutes them.
proof: The group algebra is the direct sum of right FH-modules tFH over a left transversal T. Tensoring with W turns each tFH summand into one copy of W. The direct-sum decomposition gives the dimension formula. For the trivial H-module, the resulting action is the permutation representation on G/H.
pitfall: Restriction keeps the vector space and uses fewer group elements; induction usually enlarges the vector space. The direct sum over cosets is a vector-space decomposition, not a decomposition into G-submodules.
prompt: For H=S₂ inside S₃, follow the three cosets. Inducing the trivial H representation gives the three-point permutation representation.

title: Frobenius reciprocity: extend or restrict

source.title: Odyssey: From Group Theory to Representation Theory

intuition: To define a group-compatible map out of an induced representation, it is enough to define it on the original subgroup copy. The rest is forced by symmetry.
explanation: The Hom-space statement works over any field. Given an H-equivariant map f from W to the restricted module V, extend it by a⊗w↦a·f(w). Conversely evaluate a G-equivariant map on 1⊗w. Over the complex numbers for finite groups, taking dimensions gives the familiar equality of character multiplicities.
proof: The extension is well-defined because ah⊗w=a⊗hw and H-equivariance gives ah·f(w)=a·f(hw). It is G-equivariant by construction. Evaluation at 1⊗w reverses this operation, so the maps are inverse linear isomorphisms. The character formula follows by identifying character inner products with dimensions of equivariant Hom-spaces.
pitfall: Reciprocity relates the multiplicity of a chosen irreducible after induction to its multiplicity after restriction. It does not assert that induction and restriction undo one another.
prompt: In S₃ with H generated by a transposition, standard restricts to trivial plus sign. Deduce that Ind(trivial)=trivial plus standard.

title: A representation is a linear group action

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7

intuition: A group can move a finite set; a representation moves vectors while respecting addition and scalar multiplication. Choosing a basis turns the action into matrices, without changing the underlying action.
explanation: This companion uses column vectors and left actions. James–Liebeck uses row vectors and right actions; translate conventions before comparing matrix products. A linear action automatically gives invertible maps because the action of g⁻¹ reverses the action of g. A representation is faithful when only the identity acts as the identity on every vector.
proof: The homomorphism equation gives the action law by applying both sides to v, and ρ(e)=I gives the identity law. Conversely a linear action defines linear maps ρ(g); the inverse action makes them invertible and the action law makes ρ a homomorphism. Its kernel records exactly those group elements invisible to the action.
pitfall: One vector being fixed does not mean a group element lies in the kernel. It must fix every vector. With column vectors the rightmost matrix acts first.
prompt: Move a vector and the coordinate frame under a permutation. Compare composing the matrices with composing the corresponding actions.

title: Turn a finite action into a vector space

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7

intuition: Replace each point of a finite G-set by an independent basis vector. A group element now moves labels and also moves any linear combination of labels.
explanation: The action on the basis extends uniquely by linearity. This separates the geometric object from the vector space built from its features. The cube’s eight vertices produce an eight-dimensional permutation representation, whereas its ordinary spatial action is three-dimensional. Different feature sets therefore reveal different representations of the same group.
proof: Both sides send eₓ to e_(ghx), so they agree on a basis. A permutation matrix has a 1 in the diagonal entry indexed by x exactly when gx=x, giving the trace formula. The kernel of the permutation representation equals the kernel of the action on X because basis vectors remain distinct.
pitfall: A drawing of three axes does not display an eight-dimensional representation faithfully as a geometric embedding. It can display its basis permutation and matrix exactly.
prompt: In the three-point example, follow a coefficient attached to one basis vector. Then compare the cube actions on vertices, edges, faces and diagonals.

title: A hidden line and a hidden plane

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7

intuition: Permuting three coordinates leaves their average unchanged. It also keeps zero-sum fluctuations at zero sum. These are two independent parts of the same representation.
explanation: For the permutation action of S₃ on R³, L is a trivial subrepresentation and W is the standard representation. A submodule must be both a vector subspace and stable under every group element. A basis adapted to L and W makes every action matrix block diagonal. The analogous complex decomposition uses C³, the same constant line and the complex sum-zero plane.
proof: Permutations fix (1,1,1) and preserve the sum of coordinates, hence preserve L and W. Every vector has the displayed decomposition. If a constant vector has zero sum, its constant is zero over R or C, so L∩W=0 and the decomposition is unique.
pitfall: Stability under one group element is not stability under the whole group unless that element generates it. Over a field of characteristic 3, the constant line lies inside the sum-zero subspace and this particular direct-sum formula fails.
prompt: Change the vector coordinates and apply different permutations. Its mean stays fixed; subtracting that mean leaves a vector in the invariant sum-zero plane.

title: The group algebra: add symmetries

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7
source.section: Chapter 6, pp. 53–59: group algebra, regular module and linear extension

intuition: The group law lets you compose symmetries; the group algebra also lets you take weighted sums of them. Its basis vectors are group elements, and multiplication extends the original group law linearly.
definition: FG=\left\{\sum_{g\in G}a_g g:a_g\in F\right\},\qquad \left(\sum_g a_g g\right)\left(\sum_h b_h h\right)=\sum_{g,h}a_gb_h(gh).
explanation: Here G is finite and F is a field, so FG has dimension |G|. A group representation extends to an algebra action by sending a weighted sum of group elements to the same weighted sum of their matrices. The regular left action permutes the basis G by left multiplication. General algebra elements need not act invertibly.
proof: Expand both a and b in the group basis. Bilinearity and ρ(gh)=ρ(g)ρ(h) make the two products equal term by term. Conversely, a unital FG-module restricts to a G-action since the basis elements g and g⁻¹ act as inverse operators.
pitfall: A group element g is a basis vector in FG, not a scalar in F. The zero algebra element cannot act invertibly on a nonzero module.
prompt: Follow how group multiplication determines products of basis elements, then how linear extension produces an action of a weighted sum.

title: The same symmetry in different coordinates

source.title: James–Liebeck, Representations and Characters of Groups (2nd ed.), supplied Chapters 4–7
source.section: Chapter 7, pp. 61–68: Definition 7.1, Proposition 7.2 and equivalence of representations

intuition: An intertwiner translates vectors between two representations without changing what any group action means. Acting then translating must equal translating then acting.
explanation: An invertible intertwiner identifies two representations. Their matrices may look different because the bases differ, while their actions have the same algebraic structure. Noninvertible intertwiners also matter: invariant kernels, invariant images and equivariant projections identify meaningful pieces.
theorem: T\text{ invertible}\Longrightarrow \rho_W(g)=T\rho_V(g)T^{-1},\qquad \ker T\le V,\ \operatorname{im}T\le W\text{ invariant}.
proof: For v in ker T, equivariance gives Tρ_V(g)v=ρ_W(g)Tv=0. For w=Tv in the image, ρ_W(g)w=Tρ_V(g)v remains in the image. If T is invertible, rearranging the intertwining equation gives simultaneous conjugacy for every g.
pitfall: A different conjugating matrix for each group element does not establish equivalence. One fixed invertible T must work for the entire group.
prompt: Compare a vector written in the standard coordinates with its constant-line and sum-zero components. Check that this one change of basis works for every permutation.

title: Why a cube has 48 symmetries

source.title: URECA Y2: Cube Symmetries and Actions — guided solutions
source.section: §1; supported by the 4 September meeting’s cube-action assignment

intuition: A cube symmetry chooses where the three coordinate axes go and chooses a sign on each. These choices yield 3!×2³=48 transformations; half preserve orientation.
explanation: Center the cube at the origin with vertices (±1,±1,±1). Every Euclidean symmetry fixes its center and permutes the six face centers, so it is a signed permutation matrix; conversely every such matrix preserves the cube. The rotation subgroup consists of the determinant-one matrices. This lesson supplies an independent argument for the selected assignment; it is not presented as an adopted research result.
proof: There are six axis permutations and eight sign choices. The determinant maps onto {±1}, so its kernel has 24 elements. The faithful action of G⁺ on the four body diagonals identifies it with S₄. Central inversion −I has determinant −1 and is central; each symmetry has a unique expression (−I)^εR with R in G⁺, proving the direct-product decomposition.
pitfall: The cube’s rotation group has 24 elements; its full Euclidean symmetry group has 48. Central inversion is not a rotation in three dimensions.
prompt: Enumerate the signed permutation matrices. Switch the determinant filter to compare the 24 rotations with all 48 symmetries.

title: One cube, four different actions

source.title: URECA Y2: First working meeting, 4 September 2026
source.section: Discussion and guidance: vertices, edges, faces, four body diagonals; independent reconstruction here

intuition: You can recognize a symmetry by following vertices, edges, faces or diagonals. Changing the feature set changes what the action can see: unoriented body diagonals cannot detect central inversion.
explanation: The full cube group acts transitively on its 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces and 4 unoriented body diagonals. Corresponding stabilizer sizes are 6, 4, 8 and 12. The rotational subgroup has stabilizer sizes 3, 2, 4 and 6. Vertex, edge and face actions of the full group are faithful; the diagonal action has a two-element kernel.
proof: Take direction vectors d₁=(1,1,1), d₂=(1,1,−1), d₃=(1,−1,1), d₄=(−1,1,1). If an orthogonal symmetry fixes all four lines, then Qdᵢ=sᵢdᵢ with sᵢ=±1. All pairwise dot products are nonzero, so preservation of dot products forces all signs equal. The vectors span R³, hence Q=±I. Only I has determinant one, giving an injection of the 24 rotations into S₄; equal orders make it an isomorphism.
pitfall: A permutation of the four body diagonals does not distinguish Q from −Q. Do not treat the full group’s diagonal action as faithful.
prompt: Select −I and switch between vertices and body diagonals: vertices move to opposites, while every unoriented diagonal remains the same.

title: Restriction to a cycle reveals eigenvalues

source.title: URECA Y2: Cyclic Restriction and Eigenvalues — guided solutions
source.section: §1; supplemented by the cube example in Cube Symmetries and Actions §2

intuition: If the only allowed symmetry is repeated application of one finite-order transformation, each complex eigendirection evolves by a single root of unity. Restriction turns the representation into independent cyclic modes.
explanation: Let V be a finite-dimensional complex representation and r an element of finite order m. On Vλ every power rᵏ acts by λᵏ; its dimension is the multiplicity of that one-dimensional cyclic representation. In the natural three-dimensional cube representation, a quarter-turn about the vertical axis has eigenvalues 1, i and −i. The real horizontal plane splits into two lines only after complexification.
proof: The relation ρ(r)^m=I makes its minimal polynomial divide X^m−1. Over C that polynomial splits with distinct roots, so ρ(r) is diagonalizable. Every eigenspace is stable under all powers of ρ(r), on which they act as the corresponding powers of its eigenvalue. Choosing a basis of each eigenspace gives the decomposition and trace formula.
pitfall: A group of order four has four complex irreducible characters, but a particular representation need not contain all four. For the natural cube quarter-turn the multiplicities are 1, 1, 0, 1 at 1, i, −1, −i.
prompt: Compare the real invariant plane with the complex eigenvalues of a quarter-turn. Verify the character values (3,1,−1,1) on e,r,r²,r³.

title: Why the cube has 48 symmetries

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: A symmetry sends each positive coordinate axis to one of six face directions. Once its three images are chosen orthogonally, every vertex has a determined destination.
definition: C=[-1,1]^3,\qquad G=\{Q\in O(3):Q(C)=C\}.\quad Qe_j=\varepsilon_j e_{\sigma(j)},\quad\sigma\in S_3,\ \varepsilon_j\in\{\pm1\}.
explanation: We center the cube at the origin and keep its size fixed. Its face centers are the six vectors ±e₁, ±e₂, ±e₃. A matrix in G permutes these centers, so it has exactly one nonzero entry in each row and column, with that entry equal to +1 or −1. These are signed permutation matrices. Conversely, every such matrix preserves the coordinate inequalities defining the cube.
proof: Choose the underlying permutation in 6 ways and the three signs in 8 ways; these choices give distinct matrices. The determinant is sgn(σ)ε₁ε₂ε₃. For each permutation, exactly four sign choices give determinant +1 and four give −1.
pitfall: 48 counts all Euclidean symmetries of the cube, including orientation reversal. Physical rotations alone give 24. The camera position does not change which matrix the cube represents.
prompt: Keep the coordinate permutation fixed and flip one sign. Which vertices move, and how does the determinant change?

title: A symmetry as a word of motions

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: Two quarter turns can build every rotational symmetry. A word records how the final symmetry was made, while its matrix records the resulting linear map.
explanation: A is a positive quarter turn about the x-axis; B is a positive quarter turn about the z-axis. Vectors are columns. In a product AB, B acts first. If the controls apply A, then B, then J, the displayed product must be JBA. Different words can represent the same group element; a breadth-first search produces a shortest word in a specified generator alphabet.
theorem: G^+=\langle A,B\rangle,\quad G=\langle A,B,J\rangle,\quad A^4=B^4=J^2=I,\quad AB\ne BA.
proof: The group generated by A and B sends e₃ to all six face directions. The stabilizer of e₃ contains I, B, B², B³. Orbit–stabilizer gives at least 24 elements, and all generated matrices lie among the 24 rotations, so equality holds. Adjoining −I gives the other determinant component. For noncommutativity, AB e₁=e₃ but BA e₁=e₂.
pitfall: A relation such as A⁴=I does not say these are all the defining relations. A shortest word is relative to the allowed alphabet and need not be unique.
prompt: Apply A then B; reset and apply B then A. Track the same colored vertex, then compare the unsimplified matrix products.

parameters.composition: left multiplication; rightmost factor acts first

title: One cube, four actions

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations

intuition: Changing what you label changes what a symmetry can be observed to do. Vertices, edges, faces, and diagonal lines are four different sets on which the same group acts.
explanation: For vertices, apply Q to the point. For an edge, apply Q to its unordered endpoint pair. For a face, apply Q to its outward unit normal. For a body diagonal, apply Q to the line through an opposite vertex pair; vectors v and −v represent the same diagonal. Each construction respects composition, so each gives a group homomorphism.
proof: Fixing every vertex fixes three linearly independent vectors. Fixing every face fixes the three positive coordinate normals. Fixing every edge fixes each vertex because a vertex is the intersection of its three incident edges. For diagonal lines, −I is invisible; if Q fixes all four lines, write Qdᵢ=εᵢdᵢ. Every pair of distinct chosen dᵢ has nonzero dot product, forcing all εᵢ equal. Three of the dᵢ are independent, giving Q=±I.
pitfall: A body diagonal is an unoriented line in this action. Treating its two endpoints as separate labels changes the action and its kernel.
prompt: Apply J=−I. Compare the induced permutations in all four views. Which view loses information?

title: Count symmetries by fixing one object

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations

intuition: First choose where one marked object goes. Then count how much freedom remains after its destination has been fixed.
definition: G_x=\{g\in G:g\cdot x=x\},\qquad G\cdot x=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\},\qquad |G|=|G\cdot x|\,|G_x|.
explanation: Both the rotational and full cube groups act transitively on each of the four object sets. In the rotational group, the stabilizer orders are 3 for a vertex, 2 for an edge, 4 for a face, and 6 for an unoriented diagonal. In the full group these become 6, 4, 8, and 12 respectively. A diagonal stabilizer may exchange its two endpoints.
proof: The map from left cosets gGₓ to orbit points g·x is well-defined and bijective: g·x=h·x exactly when h⁻¹g∈Gₓ. Thus the orbit has index [G:Gₓ]. The cube actions are transitive, and substituting their sizes gives the listed stabilizer orders.
pitfall: Fixing an edge setwise allows its endpoints to swap. Fixing a face setwise does not require its four vertices to remain individually fixed.
prompt: Select one face and show only its stabilizer. Use its four rotations to explain the factorization 24=6×4.

title: Why cube rotations are S₄

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: Four diagonal lines look too sparse to record a three-dimensional motion. For rotations, however, their permutation remembers the entire motion.
explanation: Use representatives d₁=(1,1,1), d₂=(1,1,−1), d₃=(1,−1,1), d₄=(−1,1,1). Our generators induce A=(1 3 4 2) and B=(1 4 2 3), with the same rightmost-first composition convention as the matrices. This correspondence translates spatial composition into permutation multiplication.
proof: The kernel of the full diagonal action is {±I}: orthogonality forces the signs on all four diagonal representatives to agree, since their pairwise dot products are nonzero. Intersecting with determinant +1 leaves only I, because det(−I₃)=−1. Thus the rotational action injects a group of order 24 into S₄, also of order 24, and is therefore an isomorphism.
pitfall: The full 48-element cube group is not S₄. Its diagonal action is two-to-one. Also, geometric determinant +1 does not imply that the induced diagonal permutation is even.
prompt: Choose a quarter turn. Its spatial determinant is +1; what is the sign of its 4-cycle on diagonal lines?

title: Separate rotation from central inversion

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: Every full cube symmetry has a unique rotational part and one extra yes-or-no choice: whether to invert all three coordinates.
explanation: If det Q=+1, take ε=0 and R=Q. If det Q=−1, take ε=1 and R=−Q. Central inversion commutes with every linear map. Its only overlap with the rotation group is the identity. These facts make the decomposition a direct product, stronger than merely splitting the set into two equal halves.
theorem: G\cong G^+\times C_2\cong S_4\times C_2,\qquad Q\longmapsto\bigl(\phi_D(Q),\det Q\bigr).
proof: The multiplication map (R,Jᵋ)↦JᵋR is a homomorphism because J is central. It is surjective by the determinant construction and injective because G⁺∩{I,J}={I}. Equivalently, the displayed map to S₄×{±1} has trivial kernel: a diagonal-kernel element is ±I, and only I has determinant +1.
pitfall: The determinant character on G is not the sign of its diagonal permutation. The two coordinates of S₄×C₂ record different information.
prompt: Hold the diagonal permutation fixed and toggle J. Observe which object actions change and why the rotation/inversion pair remains unique.

title: Orthogonality preserves geometry

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: An orthogonal matrix moves an orthonormal frame to another orthonormal frame. It preserves lengths and angles while possibly reversing handedness.
definition: O(n)=\{Q\in M_n(\mathbb R):Q^TQ=I\},\qquad SO(n)=\{Q\in O(n):\det Q=1\}.
explanation: The equation QᵀQ=I means the columns form an orthonormal basis. It gives (Qu)·(Qv)=u·v for every pair of vectors. Determinant separates the two possible orientations. A reflection in the plane perpendicular to a unit vector n has matrix Hₙ=I−2nnᵀ. In three dimensions, central inversion −I reverses orientation but is not a plane reflection.
proof: Taking determinants in QᵀQ=I gives (det Q)²=1. Multiplicativity makes determinant a homomorphism. Hₙ fixes the plane n⊥ pointwise and sends n to −n, so its determinant is −1; by contrast, −I₃ fixes no nonzero vector. A continuous path inside O(n) has constant determinant because a continuous map from an interval into {±1} is constant.
pitfall: An animation from I to an orientation-reversing matrix cannot remain a continuous path of orthogonal matrices. A morph that collapses the cube is an illustration, not a rigid motion.
prompt: Compare a plane reflection with central inversion. Display each fixed subspace and the determinant.

title: The circle group and its reflections

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: Plane rotations add angles. Adding a reflection creates a second component that reverses the direction in which angles compose.
explanation: Every element of SO(2) is exactly one Rθ modulo 2π. Every determinant −1 element of O(2) is RθF. It is reflection in the line making angle θ/2 with the x-axis. The relation FRθF=R−θ explains why O(2) is noncommutative although SO(2) is commutative. Restricting θ to multiples of 2π/n recovers the rotational and full symmetry groups of a regular n-gon.
theorem: SO(2)\cong\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z),\qquad O(2)\cong SO(2)\rtimes C_2,\qquad FR_\theta F=R_{-\theta}.
proof: The first column of an orthogonal 2×2 matrix is (cos θ,sin θ). The second unit column perpendicular to it is either (−sin θ,cos θ) or its negative; these give Rθ and RθF. Direct multiplication proves angle addition and the conjugation relation. The reflection subgroup intersects SO(2) trivially and every element has one of these two forms.
pitfall: RθF is reflection through angle θ/2, not θ. The semidirect product is not a direct product: reflection generally does not commute with rotation.
prompt: Compare FRθ with RθF while increasing θ. At which angles do the two transformations coincide?

title: SO(3): an axis and a turning angle

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: A three-dimensional rotation leaves an axis fixed and rotates its perpendicular plane. The cube rotation group selects just 24 points from this continuous family.
explanation: Rodrigues’ formula separates a vector into its component along n and its component perpendicular to n. The first stays fixed; the second undergoes a plane rotation. Every element of SO(3) has this form. Choose 0≤θ≤π: a nonidentity rotation determines an axis line, but at θ=π the choices n and −n give the same matrix. At θ=0 every axis gives the identity.
proof: A real orthogonal 3×3 matrix has eigenvalues of modulus one and nonreal eigenvalues occur in conjugate pairs. Determinant +1 forces at least one eigenvalue +1. Its unit eigenvector n has an invariant orthogonal complement, where the restriction has determinant +1 and hence is a plane rotation. Decomposing into n and n⊥ gives Rodrigues’ formula and the trace identity.
pitfall: The trace determines the angle in [0,π] but not the axis. Generic SO(3) rotations do not preserve the cube. Linear interpolation of rotation matrices is generally not orthogonal.
prompt: Rotate about a body diagonal continuously. Which angle values return the cube to its original set of occupied points?

title: Turn a set action into linear algebra

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original examples

intuition: Give each labeled object its own basis vector. A group that permutes the objects now acts linearly on all weighted combinations of those objects.
explanation: The permutation representation on cube vertices has dimension 8, even though the cube is drawn in three-dimensional space. The geometric representation acts on ℝ³ and is a different representation of the same group. A representation becomes a left module over the group algebra k[G] by extending the action linearly: formal sums of group elements act as corresponding sums of linear maps.
theorem: \left(\sum_g a_g g\right)\!\cdot v=\sum_g a_g\rho(g)v,\qquad \{k[G]\text{-modules}\}\leftrightarrow\{k\text{-linear representations of }G\}.
proof: The action law on basis vectors gives ρ(g)ρ(h)eₓ=e_{g·(h·x)}=e_{(gh)·x}; linearity proves it on all vectors. Conversely, in a unital k[G]-module each basis group element g acts invertibly, since g⁻¹ acts as its inverse. Associativity of the module action is exactly the homomorphism law.
pitfall: A representation need not be faithful, and its dimension need not equal the dimension of the picture or the size of the group. A group algebra element is a formal linear combination, not a single symmetry.
prompt: Compare the 3×3 geometric matrix with the 8×8 vertex permutation matrix of the same quarter turn.

title: Invariant subspaces are persistent patterns

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original examples

intuition: A pattern of weights is an invariant mode when every allowed symmetry keeps it inside the same family of patterns. The individual vector may move; the family survives.
definition: W\le V\text{ is }G\text{-invariant}\iff\rho(g)W\subseteq W\quad(\forall g\in G).
explanation: Label a square’s vertices 0,1,2,3 cyclically and let its full symmetry group act on ℝ⁴ by permuting basis vectors. Three invariant pieces are T=span(1,1,1,1), L=span(1,−1,1,−1), and U={(a,b,−a,−b):a,b∈ℝ}. T is the constant pattern, L alternates signs, and U contrasts opposite vertices. Quarter turns may multiply a vector in L by −1; that still preserves L.
theorem: \mathbb R^4=T\oplus L\oplus U,\qquad\dim T=1,\quad\dim L=1,\quad\dim U=2.
proof: A quarter turn and the reflection i↦−i generate the square group. Their coordinate permutations preserve T, L, and U by direct substitution. These three spaces are pairwise orthogonal for the standard dot product, and their dimensions sum to 4, proving the direct sum. The quarter turn acts on U as a 90° plane rotation, which has no invariant real line; hence U is irreducible over ℝ.
pitfall: Invariant means stable as a subspace under every group element. It does not mean every vector is fixed, and stability under one chosen symmetry alone is insufficient.
prompt: Choose a vector with four vertex weights. Decompose it into constant, alternating, and opposite-contrast parts, then apply a quarter turn.

title: Irreducibility depends on the field

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original examples

intuition: A real rotation has no real eigenline unless its angle is 0 or π. Over the complex numbers, the same matrix splits into two one-dimensional eigenmodes.
explanation: This representation on ℝ² is irreducible: a proper nonzero real invariant subspace would have to be a line. After extending scalars to ℂ, the eigenvalues are ω and ω⁻¹, where ω=exp(2πi/3), and the representation splits into their eigenspaces. Complex eigenvectors should be displayed by their real and imaginary components or phases, rather than as ordinary lines in the original real plane.
theorem: \mathbb R^2\text{ is irreducible over }\mathbb R,\qquad\mathbb C^2=E_\omega\oplus E_{\omega^{-1}},\qquad\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}.
proof: The characteristic polynomial is t²+t+1, whose discriminant is −3; hence there is no real eigenvalue or real invariant line. Over ℂ it has the two distinct roots ω and ω⁻¹. Their eigenspaces are one-dimensional, invariant under the generator, and therefore invariant under all of C₃.
pitfall: “Every irreducible representation of an abelian group is one-dimensional” requires hypotheses such as finite-dimensional representations over an algebraically closed field. It is false over ℝ as stated.
prompt: Inspect the fixed real axis, the real rotation plane and the two complex eigenvalues. Which complex eigenlines have no real counterpart?

title: Average to reveal invariant complements

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory
source.section: §3.1 and §3.6: Maschke and invariant inner products

intuition: A random projection onto an invariant subspace may favor one viewpoint. Averaging all its symmetry-transformed versions removes that preference.
explanation: Let V be finite-dimensional and W a G-invariant subspace. Choose any linear projection P onto W. The averaged map P_G still projects onto W and now commutes with the whole action. Its kernel gives an invariant complementary subspace. Repeating this splitting produces a direct sum of irreducible representations.
proof: Every conjugated projection maps into W and is the identity on W, so the average has the same two properties and is idempotent. Conjugating the sum by ρ(h) merely reindexes its terms; hence it commutes with the action. Its kernel is therefore invariant. Finite dimension lets us split recursively until all nonzero summands are irreducible.
pitfall: The division by |G| is essential. In characteristic p, the representation of Cₚ with generator [[1,1],[0,1]] has an invariant line but no invariant complementary line.
prompt: Select the constant component of a square-weight vector. Compare its mean before and after applying r or s; averaging over all eight group elements gives that projection.

title: Characters measure the action economically

source.title: Etingof et al. — Introduction to Representation Theory; original cube calculations

intuition: A character compresses each matrix to its trace. For a permutation representation this simply counts the labeled objects left in place.
explanation: For complex representations of a finite group, irreducible characters are orthonormal under the class-function inner product, and their inner products with χV give multiplicities. The five S₄ conjugacy classes have cycle types 1⁴, 2·1², 2², 3·1, and 4. The geometric cube rotation representation has character (3,−1,−1,0,1), whereas the zero-sum part of the diagonal permutation representation has character (3,1,−1,0,−1). They differ by the sign character.
proof: For a permutation matrix, a diagonal entry equals 1 exactly when that basis object is fixed, proving the fixed-point formula. Trace is unchanged by conjugation, so characters are class functions. Proof idea for the multiplicity formula: average the action on Hom(U,V) to project onto equivariant maps; its trace is the displayed inner product. Complete reducibility and Schur’s lemma identify that dimension with the multiplicity of irreducible U.
pitfall: Character values are not always nonnegative or integers. Fixed-point counting applies specifically to permutation representations. Equal dimensions do not imply equivalent representations.
prompt: Compare a face quarter turn in the geometric and diagonal permutation representations. Explain their different traces.

title: Faithful and transitive ask different questions

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations

intuition: Transitivity asks whether every position is reachable. Faithfulness asks whether every nonidentity symmetry can be detected somewhere. Neither condition forces the other.
explanation: The full cube group on its four diagonal lines is transitive but not faithful: central inversion fixes every line. Its action on the disjoint union of vertices and face centers is faithful but not transitive, because a symmetry preserves each of those two sets. The usual vertex action is both faithful and transitive. Thus reachability and detectability describe independent properties of an action.
proof: An element belongs to the kernel of the homomorphism into S_X exactly when its induced permutation is the identity, which means fixing every point. This gives the intersection formula. The cube examples then establish the claimed distinctions: inversion witnesses a nontrivial diagonal kernel, and vertex faithfulness persists after adjoining a separate orbit of face centers.
pitfall: A transitive action need not be free. The rotation group is transitive on eight vertices but every vertex still has a three-element stabilizer.
prompt: Choose vertices + faces, then follow a vertex and a face. The action is faithful but has two orbits. Compare it with the transitive diagonal action, whose full-group kernel is nontrivial.

title: A stabilizer is local; a kernel is global

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations

intuition: A stabilizer describes what one chosen object cannot detect. Intersecting stabilizers asks what the entire observation system cannot detect.
explanation: For a transitive action, choose x and set H=Gₓ. The action is equivalent to left multiplication on G/H. A single stabilizer H need not be normal: moving the chosen object conjugates its stabilizer. The kernel is the largest normal subgroup contained in H. In the rotation action on a face, H has order 4 while the kernel is trivial.
theorem: G/H\longrightarrow G\cdot x,\quad gH\longmapsto g\cdot x\quad\text{is a }G\text{-equivariant bijection}.
proof: The coset map is well-defined and bijective by the stabilizer criterion h⁻¹g∈H. An element a fixes every coset gH exactly when agH=gH for all g, equivalently g⁻¹ag∈H for all g. This is the intersection of all conjugates of H. Any normal subgroup inside H lies in every such conjugate, proving the largest-normal-subgroup statement.
pitfall: A nontrivial stabilizer does not mean the action is unfaithful. Kernel elements must fix every object, rather than just the selected one.
prompt: Pick two different faces and compare their stabilizers. Find a rotation in one stabilizer but not the other, then intersect all six.

title: Let a group act on itself in two ways

source.title: Pavel Etingof — Groups Around Us; original coordinate examples

intuition: Left multiplication moves every group element uniformly. Conjugation instead changes the frame in which a symmetry is described, preserving its structural type.
explanation: The left regular action is faithful, free, and transitive: any group element can be moved to any other in exactly one way. In the conjugation action, orbits are conjugacy classes, the stabilizer of x is its centralizer C_G(x), and the kernel is the center Z(G). For cube rotations, conjugation carries a rotation axis to the transformed axis while preserving the rotation angle.
proof: If gx=x, cancellation gives g=e; and yx⁻¹ is the unique element carrying x to y by left multiplication. For conjugation, gxg⁻¹=x exactly when gx=xg, giving the centralizer. Fixing every x is exactly membership in the center. Orbit–stabilizer then gives the conjugacy-class size.
pitfall: A left coset and a conjugacy class are different kinds of subsets. Conjugation is not generally transitive, and the identity always forms a singleton orbit.
prompt: Select a quarter turn and conjugate it by different cube symmetries. Track the axis. Then compare the result with ordinary left multiplication.

title: Count cube colorings by fixed colorings

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations

intuition: Dividing the number of colorings by the group order fails when some colorings have extra symmetry. Burnside’s average automatically accounts for these smaller orbits.
explanation: Color the six faces independently from k labeled colors, allowing repetition and allowing some colors to be unused. A coloring is fixed by a symmetry exactly when it is constant on each cycle of that symmetry’s face permutation. For rotations, the face cycle types and counts are 1⁶:1, 1²2²:3, 1²4:6, 2³:6, and 3²:8. Including orientation reversal gives a different equivalence relation.
proof: Double-count pairs (g,x) with g·x=x. Summing over g gives the fixed-point sum. Summing over each orbit gives |orbit|×|stabilizer|=|G|, so division counts orbits. Each face-permutation cycle independently receives one of k colors. Substituting the exactly enumerated cycle types yields the two polynomials. As checks, N₊(2)=N(2)=10, while N₊(3)=57 and N(3)=56.
pitfall: These formulas do not require every color to appear. Prescribed color multiplicities need a different fixed-coloring count. Averaging only the 24 improper symmetries is not Burnside’s lemma because they are not a subgroup.
prompt: Use three colors and compare rotations-only with all symmetries. Locate a pair of rotational coloring orbits merged by an orientation-reversing symmetry.

title: Read the same motion through different cycles

source.title: Donu Arapura — More counting problems with groups; original cube calculations

intuition: One quarter turn is simultaneously a permutation of 8 vertices, 12 edges, 6 faces, and 4 diagonal lines. The cycle patterns expose different features of the same motion.
explanation: A face quarter turn has vertex cycle type 4², edge type 4³, face type 1²4, and diagonal type 4. Its two fixed faces are obvious only in the face view, yet every view detects order four. Central inversion has order two on vertices, edges, and faces but acts identically on the four diagonal lines. An action can hide part or all of an element’s order.
proof: A permutation returns every point to its start exactly when the exponent is divisible by every cycle length, proving the least-common-multiple formula. Restrict φ_X to the cyclic subgroup generated by g. Its kernel is the displayed intersection, so the first isomorphism theorem gives the order formula. In a faithful action the denominator is one, and every element’s order is preserved.
pitfall: A fixed face in a set action is a face preserved as a whole; its individual points may rotate. The order of an observed permutation equals the group-element order only when the restricted action detects all its powers.
prompt: Compare B and J in all four action views. Recover their orders from cycle lengths and explain the exception for J on diagonals.
